name: Mathnasium
line: Mathnasium teaches a learning plan in sessions. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review happen at every problem.
description: AMP vs Mathnasium: Mathnasium teaches a plan set by assessment, in sessions. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous, at every problem.
verdict: Mathnasium assesses a learner at enrollment, builds a learning plan from the result, and teaches it in sessions with a live instructor [1][2]. In AMP, assessment and teaching are continuous. Every answer updates the learner's level and sets the next problem, and each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test. Every answer, right or wrong, updates the learner's level in that part of math and sets the next problem: new work within reach, a gap to close, or an old skill due back. Mathnasium assesses a learner at enrollment, in writing and out loud, and builds a learning plan from the result [1][2]. One center describes a Progress Check partway through the plan, and a new assessment before a new plan [6].

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything a learner needs hangs off the problem in front of them: a hint that gives the first step, a lesson with a worked example, a film where there is one, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In Mathnasium the unit is the session. An instructor teaches the plan, in a center or online, and the company recommends two to three sessions a week and assigns no homework [1][7]. Across 55 studies, worked examples improve performance in math [12].

reasons.title: Help is recorded, not forbidden
reasons.body: In AMP an answer given after a hint or a lesson is marked as helped and does not count as learned. A skill counts when the learner gets it right without help, more than once. So help stays in reach at every problem. In Mathnasium, a learner shows mastery on a separate check done without the instructor's help. One center describes it coming after 10 to 20 pages on a skill [5][6].

reasons.title: Continuous review
reasons.body: In AMP, learned skills come back in ordinary practice, at growing intervals, mixed with other math. One Mathnasium center describes how it checks retention: a Progress Check about halfway through a learning plan, a Post-Assessment at its end, and skills not yet mastered folded into the next plan [6]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [10].

reasons.title: A level for each part of math
reasons.body: AMP keeps a separate level for each part of math, from counting through precalculus. A learner further along in geometry than in fractions gets work at both levels, and repeated misses send practice back to what a skill builds on. Mathnasium's method is laid out in levels: seven of number sense, then algebra readiness, then algebra and higher math [2]. One center describes a Post-Assessment at the end of a plan, where 85% marks a level as mastered [6].

rows.range: Kindergarten through grade 12 [1]. Seven levels of number sense, then algebra readiness, then algebra and higher math [2].
rows.start: A separate written and verbal assessment at enrollment, which can cover topics school has not reached yet [1][4].
rows.teaching: A live instructor in sessions, in a center or online [1][7], using mental, visual, verbal, hands-on and written work [2].
rows.next: A learning plan built from the assessment [1][2]. One center turns each missed question into a skill and works on three skills at a time [6].
rows.mastery: A mastery check done without the instructor's help. One center gives it after 10 to 20 pages on a skill [5][6].
rows.review: Checked at milestones, in one center's account: a Progress Check partway through a plan and a Post-Assessment at its end [6].
rows.print: Work is done in sessions; one center says its pages are on iPads [6]. No homework is assigned [1].
rows.adult: An instructor teaches and grades the work [2][5]. No homework is assigned [1].
rows.reports: One center sends parents a monthly progress report, with attendance and skills mastered and remaining, and makes a monthly call [6].
rows.evidence: Results-page percentages with no sample or method [3]. We found no Evidence for ESSA entry and no What Works Clearinghouse intervention report [8][9].

theirs: Mathnasium is a chain of after-school math learning centers. It was founded in Los Angeles in 2002, and most centers are franchises [5]. It also teaches live online, through Mathnasium@home [7]. It serves kindergarten through grade 12 and describes itself as an after-school mathematics program [1][4].

A learner starts with a written and verbal assessment, and the center builds a customized learning plan from it [1][2]. An instructor teaches for understanding, starting from what the learner already knows, with mental, visual, verbal, hands-on and written work [2]. Mathnasium recommends two to three sessions a week, sets aside part of each session for school homework, and assigns no homework [1]. One center describes the cycle: three skills at a time, a mastery check on each, a Progress Check partway through the plan, and a Post-Assessment at the end [6].
credit: A live instructor teaches with talk, pictures, writing and physical objects, starting from what the learner already knows [2].
A person places the learner, in writing and out loud, and the assessment can reach past what school has taught [1][4].
Mastery is checked without help before a learner moves on [5][6].

theirs: Mathnasium's results page, under the heading "Proven Outcomes", gives three numbers: 94% of parents report improved skills and understanding, 93% report an improved attitude, and 90% of students saw improved school grades [3]. The page gives no sample size, method, date or comparison group.

Its FAQ says multiple independent studies found better scores on standards-based tests, but it names no study and gives no sample or result [1]. We found no entry for Mathnasium in Evidence for ESSA and no What Works Clearinghouse intervention report [8][9].

Tutoring as a whole has been studied widely. Across 263 randomized trials the average effect was 0.40 standard deviations, and 0.16 to 0.22 for large U.S. programs measured on standardized tests [11]. Those are averages across many tutoring programs, not results for Mathnasium.
ours: The two findings AMP leans on hardest: worked examples improve math performance across 55 studies [12], and practice that mixes and spaces topics scored 62% against 38% for practice in blocks a month later, in a randomized trial that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations [10]. AMP applies both at every problem.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and the code is public.

them: Your child learns best by talking math through with a person and handling real objects.
amp: You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice, with no separate tests.
You want a hint, a lesson and the worked answer at every problem.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in practice.
Your learner is at different levels in different parts of math.
Your child goes to Mathnasium and you want checked practice between sessions.

questions.question: How is AMP different from Mathnasium?
questions.answer: Mathnasium assesses a learner, builds a learning plan, and teaches it in sessions with an instructor [1][2]. AMP has no separate test: every answer sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does Mathnasium work?
questions.answer: Its results page reports percentages with no sample or method [3]. Its FAQ cites independent studies but names none [1]. We found no entry in Evidence for ESSA and no What Works Clearinghouse intervention report [8][9].

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs, and Mathnasium assigns no homework [1]. AMP places a learner from their first answers, whatever else they use.
